title: The Princess on the Glass Hill
place: A hillside farm and the king’s glass hill
sourceTitle: Popular Tales from the Norse, “Princess on the Glass Hill”
sourceAuthor: Peter Christen Asbjørnsen and Jørgen Moe; translated by George Webbe Dasent
note: A condensed reading copy of Dasent’s public-domain English translation in the cited 1903 edition. It retains Boots’s three St John’s Eve watches, the brass, silver, and gold horses, the three rides up the glass hill, and the golden-apple recognition. Repetition and crowd detail are shortened; spelling and punctuation are lightly modernized. The illustrations are newly generated because the cited edition supplies no suitable story plates.

rights.basis: The cited 1903 David Douglas edition was published before 1931 and is public domain in the United States.

artLabel: Boots discovers the golden horse that has been eating the farm’s hay.
scenes: A farmer’s meadow was eaten bare every St John’s night. His two elder sons each tried to keep watch, but when the barn shook and thundered they fled. The third son, whom everyone called Boots, stayed through three dreadful shakings until all grew still.

Outside stood a magnificent horse eating the hay, with brass armour and harness beside it. Boots threw the steel from his tinderbox over the horse, making it tame, and hid it safely. On the next two St John’s Eves he kept watch again and won still finer horses, one with silver gear and one with gold.

The king proclaimed that whoever could ride up a steep hill smooth as glass and take the three golden apples from the princess at its summit should marry her and receive half the kingdom. Princes and knights came from every side, but their horses slipped at the foot.

Boots’s brothers went to watch and mocked him for staying home in the ashes. Secretly Boots put on the brass armour and rode the brass horse one-third of the way up the hill. The princess was delighted, but the unknown knight turned and vanished.
At the second trial Boots wore silver and rode two-thirds of the way. The princess tossed one golden apple after him, and it rolled into his shoe. Again he disappeared before anyone learned his name.

On the third day Boots came in golden armour upon the golden horse. Horse and rider flashed like sunlight. They climbed the glass hill as though it were level ground, and the princess gladly placed the remaining apples in his hand.

The king summoned every man in the realm so the princess might identify the knight. Boots’s brothers came proudly, but Boots arrived last in his sooty clothes. When asked whether he had the apples, he drew all three golden apples from his pocket.
Then Boots put on the golden armour, and everyone knew him as the rider who had reached the summit. The princess chose him gladly. They celebrated their wedding, and Boots received half the kingdom.

pageArt.alt: The princess waits with three golden apples atop the gleaming glass hill as the gathered riders find its foot too slippery.
The silver-armoured rider climbs the shining glass hill toward the princess and her golden apples.
The princess gladly places a golden apple in Boots’s hand after his radiant horse climbs the glass hill with ease.
At sunrise the princess gives the victorious golden rider the final apple.
